title: Act 8: 57 Days, and a Tax Holiday in Persia

beats.text: His name was *Nadir Shah*, and he'd noticed what everybody had noticed,
which was that the Mughal Empire was now a very rich man *with no lock on his door*.
He crushed the Mughal army at *Karnal* in *1739* and entered Delhi.
At first it was orderly.
Then a rumour spread through the city that Nadir Shah had been killed, and a mob attacked his soldiers.
Several thousand were killed.
His response was to order a general massacre. For one day, his army killed in the streets of Delhi.
Estimates run to around *30,000 people*.
Then he spent the next weeks emptying the city. The imperial treasury. The jewels.
And the *Peacock Throne*, with the *Koh-i-Noor* still in it,
which is why that diamond then travelled from *Persia* to *Afghanistan* to *Punjab* and eventually to *London*,
where it sits in the *Tower of London* today.
He took so much back to Persia that he cancelled taxation there for *three years*.
One robbery. Three years of a national *tax holiday*.
The Mughal Empire technically continued for another 120 years, but *only technically*.
Real power broke apart across the map.
The *Marathas*, those raiders from the Deccan, became the biggest force in India and pushed all the way north to Delhi.
And then in *1761*, at *Panipat*, the same field where Babur had founded the empire,
the Marathas met an Afghan invasion force and lost catastrophically.
Tens of thousands dead in a single day.
It didn't destroy them, but it broke the momentum at the exact moment they might have replaced the Mughals entirely.
So now picture the board. The old empire is a shell. The strongest challenger has just been mauled.
Dozens of regional powers are circling each other, and every one of them needs money and modern weapons to fight the others.
And sitting on the coast, with money and modern weapons, is *a business*.
Not a country. A business, with *shareholders*, in *London*.

title: Act 9: The Company That Bought a Country

beats.text: The *East India Company* arrived in the 1600s to trade. Cotton, silk, spices, saltpetre, and tea.
For about 150 years, that's genuinely all it did, from a few fortified coastal warehouses, with permission from Indian rulers.
Then it noticed that Indian rulers were now fighting each other constantly,
and that both sides in any given fight would pay well for trained troops and artillery.
So the Company started *renting out soldiers*.
Then it started picking which side won.
Then it started picking *who the ruler was*.
The turning point was *Bengal* in *1757*. Bengal was the richest province in India,
and its young ruler, *Siraj-ud-Daulah*, was fed up with the Company fortifying its base without permission,
so he marched on it and took it.
The Company sent *Robert Clive* with about *3,000 men* to take it back.
Siraj had around *50,000*.
Clive didn't beat that army. *He bought it*.

beats.speaker: A
beats.text: Their commander is named Mir Jafar. He commands roughly a third of their forces.

beats.speaker: B
beats.text: And is he happy in his work?

beats.speaker: A
beats.text: He is not. He would rather be ruler himself.

beats.speaker: B
beats.text: How much does "rather" cost?

beats.speaker: A
beats.text: Sir, we have three thousand men. They have fifty.

beats.speaker: B
beats.text: Which is why I'm asking about the price rather than the tactics.

beats.speaker: A
beats.text: And if he takes the money and fights anyway?

beats.speaker: B
beats.text: Then we're in exactly the situation we're already in.

beats.speaker: A
beats.text: That's grimly logical.

beats.speaker: B
beats.text: Write to him. Be generous. Mention the throne.

beats.speaker: A
beats.text: Do we intend to actually give him the throne?

beats.speaker: B
beats.text: We intend to give him the chair.
At *Plassey*, Mir Jafar's section of the army simply stood still and watched.
Siraj's forces collapsed.
Mir Jafar got the throne and the Company got Bengal,
which within a few years meant the Company had the right to collect the taxes of *30 million people*.
A corporation with shareholders now had tax authority over a population *larger than Britain's*.
And it had its own army, which grew to roughly *a quarter of a million men*,
about *twice the size* of the British Army itself.
Then came *1770*. The rains failed in Bengal, and famine hit.
Around 10 million people died, roughly a third of the province.
And during it, the Company's tax collection didn't stop.
In some districts it went up, because the Company had revenue targets and shareholders expecting a dividend.
That's the point where a lot of people back in Britain started asking what exactly this thing was,
and Parliament began slowly taking control of it.
But it took another *eighty-seven years*, and it took soldiers refusing to bite a cartridge.
Quick note. If you're finding this useful, subscribing helps a lot, and it costs slightly less than *a province*.

title: Act 10: The Grease and the Last Emperor

beats.text: By *1857*, most of the Company's army in India was Indian.
Hundreds of thousands of Indian soldiers, called *sepoys*, with a thin layer of British officers on top.
There was already a long list of grievances.
Kingdoms were being annexed on legal technicalities whenever a ruler died without a biological son.
Soldiers were being sent overseas, which broke caste rules for many of them. Pay and promotion were capped.
Then the Company issued a *new rifle*.
To load it, you had to bite open a paper cartridge that was greased to keep it waterproof.
And a rumour spread through the barracks that the grease was made from *cow fat* and *pig fat*.
Cows are sacred to Hindus. Pigs are forbidden to Muslims.
One cartridge managed to offend *essentially everybody*.
Whether the rumour was true has been argued about for 170 years. It didn't matter.
Men believed it, and they believed it because they already believed everything else.
In March 1857 a sepoy named *Mangal Pandey* attacked his officers and was hanged.
By May, regiments were rising across northern India.
And here's the part that made the British genuinely afraid: the rebels marched to Delhi, walked into the *Red Fort*,
and declared the old, powerless, 82-year-old Mughal emperor *Bahadur Shah Zafar* their leader.
Zafar was a poet. He wrote in Urdu, he was frail, and he had been living on a British pension in a palace he did not control.
He did not ask for this. He was handed an empire he had no ability to run.
The fighting lasted more than a year and was savage on both sides. The British retook Delhi, and the reprisals were brutal.
Zafar's sons were shot.
He was put on trial and exiled to *Rangoon*, in Burma,
where he died in 1862 and was buried in an unmarked grave so that his tomb could never become a shrine.
A famous line attributed to him laments a man who cannot find even two yards of ground for burial in the land he loved.
beats.fix: Script presented the 'two yards' couplet as definitely his; scholars dispute the attribution, so it is now 'attributed to him'.

beats.text: The last Mughal emperor, descendant of Babur and Akbar, died a prisoner in another country.
After 1857, the British Crown took India directly from the Company. Queen Victoria became *Empress of India*.
The *Raj* had begun. And it built things.
Roughly *60,000 kilometres* of railway, one of the largest networks on Earth,
plus telegraph lines, canals and universities.
But look at the *other number*.
Around 1700, India produced something like *a quarter* of the world's economic output.
By 1950, it was around *four percent*.
Indian textiles, which had clothed the world for centuries, were priced out by British factory cloth
while Indian raw cotton was shipped out to feed those same factories.
And then a lawyer got thrown off a train in *South Africa*.
